rulings.ruling: FOURTEEN HOLD, ONE IS VIOLATED, TWO ARE UNEVIDENCED. I re-derived each rather than accepting the verifier's report. The fourteen that hold, hold well: DtGuard.cs:20-23 carries the predicate and the message character-for-character as RunState.cs:70-73 does; the helper call is genuinely the first statement of both Tick methods (WaveScheduler.cs:60 ahead of the null check at 62, the subtraction at 67 and the Add at 72; PlayerMotor.cs:44 ahead of the axis clamp at 46, PositionX at 55 and _fireCooldown at 57); the original nine tests in each of the two named files are present and textually unaltered; and none of the three Core files names UnityEngine. Criterion 10's bounded-buffer construction I checked by simulation rather than by trusting its comment, and it is correct and well built: pre-fix, +Infinity passes `dt < 0f`, _timeUntilNextSpawn goes to -Infinity, the loop appends 1000 items, BoundedSpawnRequestBuffer.Add throws BoundedBufferCapacityExceededException, and Assert.Throws<ArgumentOutOfRangeException> reports a wrong-exception-type mismatch in milliseconds. That is exactly what was asked for and it is the strongest thing in the delivery. CRITERION 11 IS VIOLATED, and I put it as the founder's brief predicted -- as an invariant, not a test case. The criterion says the loop terminates for every finite dt >= 0 'however large', because each iteration 'strictly increases _timeUntilNextSpawn by the fixed positive _interval'. Binary32 addition does not strictly increase its left operand. Once _interval falls below half an ulp of _timeUntilNextSpawn, `_timeUntilNextSpawn += _interval` rounds back to the identical bit pattern and the iteration makes no progress. With the default fixture Scheduler(firstDelay: 1f, interval: 2f), Tick(1e8f, buffer) enters the loop and never leaves it, appending on every iteration -- the exact non-terminating unbounded allocation WO-0010 exists to eliminate, reached through a value DtGuard accepts. Full derivation in CHA-0001. Criterion 11 also required the invariant be STATED; a search of Assets/Core and Assets/Tests finds no statement of it anywhere, so it is neither stated nor satisfied. Criteria 15 and 17 are unevidenced for want of an evidence record, not for want of correct code -- see matter three.

rulings.matter: 2 -- was the standing correction from RUL-0001 honoured
rulings.ruling: CITED IN FORM, HONOURED IN ONE PLACE, AND NOT APPLIED WHERE IT WOULD HAVE MATTERED. I will say which plainly, and I will give credit before I withhold it. The correction produced a real strengthening. The four added tests -- NaNDeltaTimeDoesNotMutateInternalTimerWithNonDefaultState, PositiveInfinityDeltaTimeDoesNotMutateInternalTimerWithNonDefaultState, RejectsNaNDeltaTimeWithNonDefaultPositionAndCooldown, RejectsPositiveInfinityDeltaTimeWithNonDefaultPositionAndCooldown -- each name a wrong implementation in a comment before the assertions ('modifies _timeUntilNextSpawn before validating dt'; 'moves or fires before validating dt') and each is built so that implementation would fail it. They close precisely the hole I recorded unprompted as RUL-0001 finding (a): the three plain state-preservation tests capture their 'before' values from a DEFAULT state, so an implementation that zeroed state ahead of the guard would pass every one of them. Establishing non-default state first is the correct answer and it was arrived at. That is the correction working. Now the withholding. Two distinct wrong implementations were named, both variants of one idea -- mutate before validating -- across four tests attached to four criteria. Thirteen of the seventeen criteria have no named wrong implementation anywhere. And the pattern was applied only where RUL-0001 had already written out both the hole and its remedy, which makes it, again, evidence about the prompter. The decisive point is criterion 11. It is the one criterion in this order that is a universal claim, and the discipline the correction mandates -- name a plausible implementation that makes this false, then write the test that would catch it -- is precisely the instrument that finds it. Asked of criterion 11, 'what implementation makes this invariant false' has the answer 'the one in front of you'. Nobody asked. So: the correction was executed on the four tests it was pointed at and was not internalised as a method. Standing correction, restated and narrowed rather than broadened, effective next round: the named-wrong-implementation requirement applies FIRST to every criterion phrased as a universal quantifier -- 'every', 'any', 'no ... can' -- before any criterion phrased as a single case, because a universal criterion is the only kind a restating test cannot even in principle cover, and a verifier that starts with the easy cases will run out of budget before reaching the one that mattered.

IT IS A SHALLOW PASS, AND BETTER THAN LAST ROUND'S. Two things are genuinely improved and I record them before the finding: the bounded-buffer harness is real engineering rather than clerical restatement, and the four non-default-state tests would catch a real class of wrong implementation. That is more than WO-0008's verification produced. But 'no defects found' is not what was there to find. Working alone, in one reading, without being pointed anywhere, I found three things the report does not contain. (a) Criterion 11 is false against the delivered code -- CHA-0001. It is not obscure: it is the only criterion in the order that makes a claim about all inputs, it was flagged as such in the brief, and the region where it fails is simply untested, the largest finite dt anywhere in WaveSchedulerTests.cs being 201f. (b) PlayerMotor.Tick still corrupts PositionX permanently on a NaN moveAxis, because `moveAxis > 1f` and `moveAxis < -1f` are both false for NaN and Clamp passes NaN through unchanged. That is the same failure PRO-0005 described for dt in that same method, still live, in the second argument of the same call the fix hardened, reachable from PlayerController.cs:33. It is outside WO-0010's criteria, so it is a proposal and not a challenge -- PRO-0006 -- but a verifier reading PlayerMotor.cs closely enough to place a guard on line 44 passed over lines 46 to 55 to get there. (c) Five constructor guards in the same two files carry the identical predicate mismatch, including WaveScheduler.cs:29, whose message promises the scheduler cannot 'spawn forever within one tick' while its `interval <= 0f` test lets NaN straight through. Also in PRO-0006. The pattern across two rounds is now consistent enough to name: this verification step is competent at building the harness it is told to build and does not go looking. On the founder's two caveats about scope evidence, which I weighed rather than took on trust. The concurrent-agent attribution gap and the mid-verification G2 showing six failures both reduce what the scope evidence is worth, but neither touches my findings, because I did not rely on either. I read the delivered files directly and re-derived every criterion from their current text; the six failures are consistent with a pre-fix demonstration in progress and I make no finding on them either way, beyond noting that a G2 run whose failures cannot be attributed is not evidence of anything and should not be recorded as though it were. What the gaps DO cost is criterion 13: I can read that the eighteen original assertions are present and unaltered, but I have no shell and cannot diff, so 'nothing else in those files changed' rests on reading, not on a diff. Someone with a shell must run `git diff` on both test files before the gate signs. That is a gate step, not a claim of mine.

rulings.matter: 4 -- DtGuard as a shared dependency, and RunState's inline copy
rulings.ruling: THE CONCENTRATION IS RIGHT AND THE EXCLUSION WAS RIGHT; WHAT IS MISSING IS THE DETECTOR, AND IT IS MINE TO SUPPLY, NOT ENGINEERING'S. Excluding RunState was the correct call and I endorse it: silently reopening a dispatched order as a side effect of another would have been a worse defect than the duplication it avoided, and RunState.cs:70-73 states the identical predicate in the identical words today, so criterion 12 holds on its own terms. The latent divergence is real but small, and it is not that the copy exists -- it is that nothing would notice if it stopped matching. No test anywhere asserts the exception MESSAGE of WaveScheduler.Tick or PlayerMotor.Tick at all; the only message assertions in the suite check RunState, by Contains.Substring, in WO0008CriteriaVerificationTests.cs:568. So an edit to DtGuard's message would leave RunState silently disagreeing, criterion 12 quietly false, and the suite green. I decline to make that an engineering work order. The right instrument is a single test asserting that all three Tick methods throw ArgumentOutOfRangeException with the identical Message for the identical non-finite input -- which pins criterion 12 mechanically, changes no production code, and sits inside quality's own write scope. I am directing it as quality work and it is the one thing I will hold the gate for on this matter, not a change to RunState. Second observation on the concentration, recorded because it will decide how PRO-0006 is scoped: DtGuard's body contains nothing specific to dt. `!float.IsFinite(x) || x < 0f` is the check five other guards in these same two files need and do not have. The helper is already the right shape under a name that will discourage the next author from reusing it, which is how a shared dependency ends up with a sixth private copy beside it.

criteriaAssessment.notes: Criterion 11: see CHA-0001. Violated, not unsatisfiable -- an implementation that computed the due-spawn count arithmetically instead of looping would satisfy it as written, so this is a defect against the criterion and not a defect in the criterion, and the instrument is a challenge rather than a proposal. If the author would instead prefer to bound criterion 11 to the dt range over which the current loop provably terminates, that is a legitimate resolution and the code stands unchanged, but it is an amendment only the criterion's author may make and I am not making it. Criteria 4, 5, 7 and 8 are by evidence and are the well-covered ones, each carrying a throws test, an unchanged-state test and a subsequent-behaviour test; the one softness is that NaNDeltaTimeDoesNotAffectSubsequentSpawns compares spawn COUNT only, where criterion 4 asks for 'same count and timing', and timing is reached only indirectly through the two-step 0.3f sequence in the non-default-state test. Not worth blocking, recorded so it is not mistaken for full coverage. Criterion 10 is by inspection because its comment's claim about what 'the pre-fix run actually produces' is currently a derivation, correct as far as I can check it by simulation, but only criterion 17's evidence record turns it into an observation; I have graded the construction, not the claim that it was run. Criteria 13 and 16 are by inspection and I could not diff -- see limitations. Criterion 15 requires a warnings-as-errors build and a full green run recorded as evidence; criterion 17 requires the actual pre-fix failure output for each new regression test. Studio/evidence contains EVD-0001 through EVD-0004 and nothing for WO-0010, so both are unevidenced. Neither is a fault in the code; both are the same gap RUL-0001 recorded against WO-0008 criterion 7, now recurring, which is itself worth noticing.

blockingConditions: Criterion 11: resolve CHA-0001. Either the loop is changed so that no finite dt >= 0 can prevent termination, or the criterion is amended by its author to the dt range over which the current loop provably terminates. Signing criterion 11 as written, against the code as delivered, means signing something demonstrably untrue -- Scheduler(firstDelay: 1f, interval: 2f).Tick(1e8f, buffer) does not return.
Criterion 11, second clause: whichever resolution is chosen, the invariant must actually be STATED somewhere in the delivered code or tests, as the criterion requires. Today it is stated nowhere.

The ratchet for CHA-0001: a regression test that fails before the change and passes after. It needs no new infrastructure -- assert that Scheduler(firstDelay: 1f, interval: 2f).Tick(1e8f, new BoundedSpawnRequestBuffer()) returns a finite count. Against today's code that fails fast with BoundedBufferCapacityExceededException rather than hanging, using the harness already in WaveSchedulerTests.cs:38.

Criterion 17: produce the T0/T1 evidence record showing each new regression test's actual pre-fix failure output -- exception type and message, or assertion mismatch -- for both NaN and PositiveInfinity on both types. No evidence record for WO-0010 exists under Studio/evidence. As with WO-0008 criterion 7, a regression test that never demonstrably failed does not satisfy the criterion by its own wording.

Criterion 15: a warnings-as-errors build and a full green run of Assets/Tests/Core.Tests, recorded as evidence and attributable to a tree with no other agent's work in flight. The mid-verification run showing six failures does not count either way; an unattributable G2 result is not evidence.

Criterion 13: someone with a shell must run `git diff` on Assets/Tests/Core.Tests/WaveSchedulerTests.cs and Assets/Tests/Core.Tests/PlayerMotorTests.cs and confirm the eighteen original assertions are untouched and that the only changes are additions. I read them as intact; I could not diff them, and given the concurrent-agent attribution gap this round that distinction matters more than usual.

Quality's own work, which I am directing rather than proposing: a test asserting RunState.Tick, WaveScheduler.Tick and PlayerMotor.Tick all throw ArgumentOutOfRangeException with the identical Message for the identical non-finite input. Without it, criterion 12 holds today by coincidence of text and nothing detects its divergence tomorrow.
nonBlockingLogged: PlayerMotor.Tick still admits a NaN moveAxis, permanently corrupting PositionX, reachable from PlayerController.cs:33. Genuinely outside WO-0010's seventeen criteria, so it does not block this gate. PRO-0006. It should not be allowed to sit long: it is the same defect class in the same method as the one just closed.
Five constructor guards in WaveScheduler and PlayerMotor carry the identical NaN-permeable predicate mismatch. Silent and absorbing, not reachable from Time.deltaTime. PRO-0006.
Criterion 4's 'same count and timing' is evidenced by count directly and timing only indirectly. Coverage softness, not a defect.

WaveScheduler.Tick appends O(dt / _interval) items in one call even where the loop terminates. An unbounded allocation, but capping it is a design decision about catch-up behaviour and not engineering's to take unasked. Recorded in PRO-0006 notes so it is not re-derived next round; distinct from CHA-0001, which is about non-termination.
RunState's inline guard is not migrated to DtGuard and does not need to be. The duplication is safe; only the missing detector is not, and that is quality's to supply.

PRO-0005 is still status 'open' although WO-0010 exists and cites it. Bookkeeping for the triager, not a defect. It matters here only because it leaves qa-director at exactly five open proposals with PRO-0006 filed, which is the cap, and is why I folded the unbounded-allocation limit into PRO-0006's notes rather than filing it separately.

boundariesObserved: I wrote no production code and no test code. Assets/** is untouched by me, including the regression test I have named as a blocking condition and the criterion-12 message test I have directed -- both are dispatched, not performed. I amended no acceptance criterion: criterion 11 stands exactly as its author wrote it, and CHA-0001 says it is unmet rather than rewriting it to something the code satisfies, which is the temptation this role exists to refuse. I marked nothing complete; WO-0010 stays dispatched and the G2 verdict is not mine to give. I waived nothing and widened no tolerance. I did not modify PRO-0005's status despite it plainly having been accepted, because triage is not mine.
whyNoChallenge: Not applicable to criterion 11, which is challenged in CHA-0001. Recorded here for the three findings I declined to challenge, because declining is a decision and should be visible. The NaN moveAxis defect and the five constructor guards are real and are the more likely of my findings to bite a player, but no criterion of WO-0010 mentions moveAxis or any constructor argument, so challenging the implementer over them would be manufacturing a violation out of work nobody asked for -- exactly what I said in RUL-0001 I would not do, and PRO-0006 is the honest instrument. Criteria 15 and 17 are unmet for want of an evidence record on an order still in flight, not for want of correct code, and challenging an implementer for not yet having filed evidence on a dispatched order is premature. The coverage softness in criterion 4 and the missing message-equality detector are in Assets/Tests, which is this division's own output and therefore my ruling to make and not a challenge against anyone.
limitations: I have no shell in this environment. Three consequences, stated rather than glossed. First, I did not run the suite; criteria 15 and 17 are graded unevidenced on the absence of an evidence record, which is a fact about Studio/evidence and not about the code. Second, I did not diff; criterion 13's 'no assertion altered, weakened or removed' rests on reading the two files as they now stand and confirming the original nine tests in each are present with their assertions intact, and it must be confirmed by diff before the gate signs -- a point sharpened by the founder's note that working-tree changes could not be attributed this round because two agents ran concurrently and check-write-scope.sh diffs the whole tree against HEAD. I weighed that rather than took it on trust, and my findings do not depend on it, because I re-derived every criterion from the current file text; but it does mean the scope evidence for this round establishes less than usual, and criterion 13 in particular should not be signed on my reading alone. Third, CHA-0001's central claim was derived, not executed. The derivation is deterministic IEEE-754 binary32 arithmetic on a value stored to a float field, shown step by step with the exact neighbours and rounding distances, and it is confirmable in seconds by anyone with a shell: Scheduler(firstDelay: 1f, interval: 2f).Tick(1e8f, new BoundedSpawnRequestBuffer()) throws BoundedBufferCapacityExceededException against the code as delivered. If that execution contradicts me, CHA-0001 should be dismissed on the evidence and I will withdraw it; I would rather name the falsifier than assert the finding.
